In 1974, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman rigged a wheel of fortune to stop at either ten or sixty five.
People who saw ten gave a median estimate of twenty five percent.
People who saw sixty five guessed forty five percent.
A number they knew was random dragged their answers.
This is anchoring.
The first number in a conversation becomes a reference point, and everything after gets measured against it.
In negotiation, that matters enormously.

In a 1987 study by Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale, professional estate agents valued the same house differently depending on the listing price they were shown, while insisting the listing price hadn't influenced them.
Research by Adam Galinsky and others suggests that, in many negotiations, the first offer strongly predicts the final deal.
That's why it often pays to go first with an ambitious but justifiable number.
If someone else anchors first, don't argue from their number.
Re anchor with your own reasoning and your own figure.
Anchors work even when we know about them.
You can't switch the bias off, but you can decide who sets the anchor.

Take a wooden ship.
Over the years, replace every plank, one by one, until none of the originals remain.
Is it still the same ship?
This puzzle is the Ship of Theseus.
The Greek writer Plutarch recorded it around two thousand years ago.
The Athenians kept the ship of their hero Theseus, replacing rotting timbers as they went, and philosophers argued about whether it was really still his ship.
Centuries later, the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes added a twist.
Suppose someone collects all the old planks you threw away and rebuilds the original ship with them.
Now there are two ships.
Which one is the real Ship of Theseus?
The puzzle gets personal fast.
Your body replaces many of its cells over time.
Your opinions, tastes and memories change.
Are you the same person you were ten years ago?
You may have heard that every cell in your body is replaced every seven years.
That's a myth.
Different cells renew at very different rates, and many neurons in your brain stay with you for life.
The philosopher John Locke argued that personal identity comes from psychological continuity, especially memory, rather than from the material you're made of.
Maybe identity isn't about the planks at all.
It's about the pattern, the story that connects past and present.
You are less a thing and more a process.

A Formula One car is shaped a bit like an aeroplane wing.
Just upside down.
Instead of lifting off the ground, it's pushed into it.
That push is called downforce.
Air flowing over and under the car, especially through the wings and the shaped floor, creates a pressure difference that presses the car onto the track.
More downforce means more grip, and more grip means faster corners.
At high speed, the downforce can be greater than the car's own weight.
That's why people often say an F1 car could, in theory, drive upside down on a ceiling.
It's never been tried, but the physics points that way.
The trade off is drag.
Downforce costs straight line speed, so teams tune their wings differently for twisty tracks like Monaco and fast ones like Monza.
Formula One is less about raw engine power than about managing air.
The fastest teams are the ones who make the air do the most work.

Rules require cars to use different dry compounds in a dry race, which forces strategic choices.
Tyres also have a working temperature window.
Too cold and they don't grip.
Too hot and they degrade fast.
Drivers spend much of a race managing that balance.
A pit stop to change all four tyres can take around two to three seconds when it goes perfectly.
A race is often won by the team that understands its tyres best, not the team with the fastest car on a single lap.

For a few laps you're much faster, and when they finally pit, you may have jumped ahead.
The opposite move, staying out longer on a clear track, is called the overcut.
Strategy turns racing into chess at three hundred kilometres an hour.

For centuries Japan had an emperor.
But often, the emperor wasn't really in charge.
From the late twelfth century, military leaders called shoguns held real power, while the emperor remained a symbolic and religious figure in Kyoto.
The Tokugawa shogunate, founded in 1603, ruled for over two and a half centuries.
Japan shows how symbolic power and real power can live side by side for centuries.
Next: the long isolation.
For centuries Japan had an emperor.
But often, the emperor wasn't really in charge.
For over two hundred years, Japan sharply limited contact with the outside world.
Under the Tokugawa, foreign trade was tightly controlled, with limited contact through places like Dejima in Nagasaki.
The policy is often called sakoku.
In 1853, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry arrived and pushed Japan to open up.
Isolation brought stability, and a shock when the world arrived.
Next: the great transformation.
For over two hundred years, Japan sharply limited contact with the outside world.
In about fifty years, Japan went from feudal domains to an industrial power.
The Meiji Restoration of 1868 returned power to the emperor and launched rapid modernisation: railways, factories, a national army and a new education system.
Japan's first railway opened in 1872, between Tokyo and Yokohama.
Change can be astonishingly fast when a society decides it must be.

It's usually not a gift.
An advance is typically paid back, or recouped, from the artist's share of royalties.
Until it's recouped, the artist may not see further royalty payments from those recordings.
Labels often also recoup certain costs, depending on the contract.
Read the deal, not the headline number.

It's usually not a gift.
Every hit song has two kinds of rights: the recording, and the composition.
The master recording is the specific recorded version.
Labels traditionally own masters in exchange for funding and marketing.
The composition, the melody and lyrics, belongs to songwriters and publishers.
That split is why an artist can re-record their old songs: they may control the composition even if they don't own the original masters.
In music, ownership is where the long-term money lives.

At the smallest scales, reality stops behaving like the world you know.
Electrons and photons can behave like particles and like waves.
In the famous double slit experiment, particles fired one at a time still build up a wave like interference pattern, as if each one explored more than one path.
Quantum mechanics is one of the most precisely tested theories in science.
Weird doesn't mean wrong.
Quantum theory is strange and incredibly well supported.
Next: superposition.
At the smallest scales, reality stops behaving like the world you know.
Superposition doesn't mean something is secretly one thing.
It means the maths describes a combination of possibilities.
Before a measurement, a quantum system is described by a combination of possible outcomes, each with a probability.
When you measure, you get one definite result.
Schrödinger's cat was invented in 1935 to show how strange this seems when scaled up.
Quantum mechanics predicts probabilities brilliantly.
What's really happening underneath is still debated.
Next: entanglement.

It means the maths describes a combination of possibilities.
Two particles can be linked so that measuring one tells you about the other, no matter how far apart they are.
Einstein called it spooky action at a distance.
Experiments have confirmed entanglement many times.
But it can't be used to send messages faster than light, because each individual result still looks random.
The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics recognised experiments on entangled photons.
The universe is more connected than common sense suggests, but it still keeps its speed limit.

You buy a cinema ticket to see a film.
But for the cinema, the film is often just the bait.
The real business is the popcorn.
When you buy a ticket, a big share of that money usually goes to the film's distributor, not the cinema.
In the opening weeks of a big release the distributor's share can be especially high.
The cinema keeps more of the ticket money the longer a film runs, but by then the crowds have often moved on.
Popcorn, though, belongs entirely to the cinema.
The ingredients cost very little.
Sell it for several pounds, and the profit margin is enormous.
That's why concessions can make up a much bigger share of a cinema's profit than their share of revenue suggests.
Then there's the sizing trick.
Ever noticed the medium popcorn costs nearly as much as the large?
That's often the decoy effect.
A middle option priced to make the bigger option look like a bargain.
Behavioural economist Dan Ariely famously described a magazine subscription offer: web only, print only, or print and web for the same price as print only.
Almost nobody wanted print only, but its presence pushed people toward the bundle.
Next time a price looks weird, ask what it's for.
Sometimes a product exists not to be bought, but to make another one look good.

In 1947, Europe was still living with rationing.
Then a designer sent out skirts that used extravagant amounts of fabric.
It was a scandal, and a sensation.
On the twelfth of February 1947, Christian Dior showed his first collection in Paris.
Wartime clothes had been boxy and practical, shaped by shortages.
Dior's silhouettes were the opposite: soft shoulders, tiny cinched waists, and full, long skirts.
The editor of Harper's Bazaar, Carmel Snow, reportedly told him: it's quite a revolution, dear Christian, your dresses have such a new look.
The name stuck.
The New Look.
Not everyone loved it.
Using so much fabric while people still faced shortages struck many as wasteful, even offensive.
In Britain, officials and politicians criticised it.
There were reports of protests in Paris.
But women wanted it, and the look spread around the world.
Some New Look skirts used many metres of fabric, at a time when British clothing rationing continued until 1949.
The New Look shows that fashion is never just about clothes.
After years of war, Dior sold something people craved: abundance, romance and the idea that normal life was back.

Some animals barely seem to age.
A naked mole rat can live over thirty years, about ten times longer than you'd predict for a rodent its size.
Scientists want to know how.
Ageing isn't one thing.

In 2013, researchers published a framework called the hallmarks of ageing, a list of biological processes that go wrong as we get older, from damaged DNA to worn down chromosome ends to cells that stop dividing but refuse to die.
An updated version in 2023 listed twelve.
Naked mole rats are a fascinating outlier.

In a 2018 study, the biologist Rochelle Buffenstein and colleagues analysed thousands of records and found that, unlike most mammals, their risk of dying didn't seem to rise with age in the way you'd expect.
And in the lab, scientists can extend lifespan in some animals.
Eating fewer calories extends life in yeast, worms and mice.
A drug called rapamycin has extended lifespan in mice.
None of this has yet been shown to extend maximum human lifespan.
The longest confirmed human life is still Jeanne Calment, who died in 1997 at one hundred and twenty two.
Here's the honest picture.
Longevity science is real and moving fast, but most headlines run far ahead of the evidence.
The best proven tools for a longer, healthier life are still deeply unglamorous: sleep, movement, not smoking, and the people around you.

The vault was two floors underground.
It had ten layers of security, including heat sensors, a magnetic field, and a lock with a hundred million possible combinations.
In February 2003, a crew beat almost all of them.
The place was the Antwerp Diamond Centre in Belgium, at the heart of the world's diamond trade.
The man later convicted as the crew's leader was Leonardo Notarbartolo, an Italian who had rented an office in the building and spent a long time quietly studying it.

According to investigators and later accounts, the crew covered a heat and motion sensor to blind it, used tricks with tape and aluminium to defeat the magnetic sensor on the vault door, and opened the combination lock with a copied key.
Over a weekend they emptied a large number of the safe deposit boxes.
The loot was estimated at over a hundred million dollars, and most of it has never been recovered.
Then came the mistake.
Near a motorway outside Brussels, some of the crew dumped a bag of rubbish in the woods.
A local man found it: torn envelopes from the diamond centre, a video tape of the vault, and a half eaten salami sandwich.
Police traced receipts and evidence back to the gang.
Notarbartolo was convicted and sentenced to ten years.
He has given his own version of events over the years, and parts of the story remain disputed.
The lesson heist stories keep teaching: security is only as strong as the most human part of it.
The crew beat the technology.
They lost to rubbish disposal.

Today salt is the cheapest thing in your kitchen.
For most of history it was so valuable that people built roads for it, taxed it, smuggled it, and rebelled over it.
Before refrigeration, salt was how you kept food from rotting.
Salted fish, salted meat and cheese could last through winter or a long sea voyage.
Control the salt, and you control the food supply.
Ancient Rome had a road called the Via Salaria, the salt road.
You've also probably heard that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, and that's where the word salary comes from.
The word does come from the Latin for salt.
But the idea that soldiers were literally paid in salt has thin evidence.
It's a great story, not a proven fact.
Salt taxes were everywhere.
In France, the hated salt tax called the gabelle was a long running grievance in the decades before the French Revolution.
And in 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led the Salt March, walking about three hundred and eighty five kilometres to the sea to make salt in defiance of British salt laws.
It became one of the most powerful protests of the independence movement.
Salt left its name all over maps.
Salzburg in Austria literally means salt castle.
When something becomes cheap, we forget it ever mattered.
Salt is a reminder to ask: what ordinary thing today is quietly running the world?

A chatbot that writes poems, explains physics and fixes code is, at its core, doing something surprisingly simple: guessing what comes next.
Large language models are a kind of neural network, a system loosely inspired by brains, made of huge numbers of adjustable values called parameters.
During training, the model reads enormous amounts of text, broken into pieces called tokens, and practises one task over and over: predict the next token.
Each time it guesses wrong, the training process nudges its parameters slightly so the right answer becomes a bit more likely.
Repeat that billions of times, and something remarkable emerges.
To predict text well, the model has to pick up grammar, facts, styles of reasoning and patterns of conversation.
After that, models are usually refined further, for example with human feedback, to be more helpful, follow instructions and avoid harmful outputs.
Because these models are trained to produce plausible text, they can sometimes generate confident statements that are wrong.
People call this hallucination.
It's why checking important facts still matters.
Calling it just next word prediction undersells it, and calling it a digital brain oversells it.
The truth is in between: a powerful pattern learner, trained at a scale that produces surprising abilities, and real limits.

In 2016, a streetwear brand sold a red clay brick with its logo on it.
It sold out.
People resold it for many times the original price.
It was a brick.
The brand was Supreme, founded by James Jebbia in New York in 1994 as a skate shop.
Its famous red box logo was inspired by the art of Barbara Kruger.
For years it stayed small, deliberately.
Supreme's model became known as the drop.
Instead of stocking huge amounts of a product, it releases small batches of new items, often on Thursdays, and lets them sell out.
Queues formed outside stores.
Online drops sold out in minutes.
Scarcity turned every release into an event.
Scarcity does something psychological.
When something might run out, we value it more, and owning it signals that you were early, in the know, part of the tribe.
The product is the T shirt.
What you're really buying is belonging.
In 2020, VF Corporation, the owner of brands like The North Face and Vans, bought Supreme for about two point one billion dollars.
In 2024, it agreed to sell it to EssilorLuxottica for about one and a half billion.
Cult brands don't just sell products.
They sell identity, and they make you feel lucky to have it.
Next time you want something because it's rare, ask whether you want the thing, or the feeling of having got it.

One of the bestselling children's books ever written uses only fifty different words.
It exists because of a bet.
Dr.
Seuss had written The Cat in the Hat using a limited vocabulary of a couple of hundred words.
His publisher, Bennett Cerf, reportedly bet him fifty dollars he couldn't write a book using just fifty different words.
Seuss took the bet.
The result, published in 1960, was Green Eggs and Ham.
Sam I am.
I do not like them.
Repetition, rhythm and a tiny vocabulary became the whole style.
It went on to become one of the bestselling children's books of all time.
It's a perfect example of a surprising truth: limits often make people more creative, not less.
Psychology research backs this up.
In studies by Catrinel Haught Tromp, people asked to write rhymes using specific given words produced work rated as more creative than people with no constraints.
Think of haiku, with their strict syllables, or songs built on just four chords.
Constraints give the mind a puzzle to solve instead of an empty page.
A blank page is terrifying because anything is possible.
Give yourself a rule, a word limit, a deadline, three colours, and suddenly your brain has something to push against.

For years, the founder of one of the most valuable companies on Earth paid himself a salary of about eighty thousand dollars.
He still became one of the richest people alive.
That founder was Jeff Bezos, whose base salary at Amazon was famously modest for many years.
His wealth didn't come from the salary.
It came from owning a large share of the company.
This is the core mechanic of extreme wealth.
Income is what you're paid for your time.
Ownership, or equity, is a claim on something that can grow without you working more hours.
A salary is capped by hours in the day.
A slice of a company can grow with every new customer.
That's also why billionaire rankings jump around.
Most of that wealth is the market value of shares.
When a company's share price swings, a founder's net worth can rise or fall by billions in a single day, without any cash changing hands.
Because selling shares can trigger taxes, some very wealthy people borrow against their shares instead of selling.
It's a strategy we'll explore later in the series.
Most people think about money as income.
Wealth is really about ownership.
You don't need to become a billionaire to use the idea: owning even small slices of productive things, like a pension invested in companies, is how ordinary people tap into the same engine.

The colour of the jumper you bought this season may have been forecast years ago, in a report you've never seen, by people you'll never meet.
Fashion trends feel spontaneous.
They're often anything but.
A whole industry of trend forecasting agencies studies runways, streets, social media, art and even economic moods to predict what colours, fabrics and shapes people will want.
Brands pay for these forecasts and design toward them, sometimes well over a year ahead.
One famous signal is Pantone's Colour of the Year, launched with Cerulean for the year two thousand.
It's part forecast, part marketing, and it ripples through products from phones to sofas.
There's an old theory about how trends move, from the sociologist Georg Simmel in 1904.
He argued fashion trickles down: elites adopt a style to stand out, others copy it, and the elites move on to something new.
Today many trends bubble up instead, from streets, subcultures and the internet, and are then picked up by big brands.
Social media has sped up the cycle dramatically.
Micro trends can rise and fade in weeks, which feeds fast fashion's constant demand for new products.
Trends aren't just about taste.
They're a system of signals about belonging and difference.
Knowing how the machine works doesn't stop you enjoying style.
It just helps you choose what's actually yours.

Right now, you're probably a bit shorter than you were this morning.
By tonight you'll have shrunk a little more.
Don't worry, you'll grow back while you sleep.
Between the bones of your spine sit intervertebral discs, squishy cushions with a tough outer ring and a gel like centre.
They're partly made of water, and they act like shock absorbers.
When you're upright, gravity and the weight of your body press down on those discs all day.
Slowly, they lose a little fluid and flatten.
Each disc only compresses a tiny bit, but you've got lots of them stacked up.
Add it together and many people lose around a centimetre of height between morning and evening.
Lie down to sleep and the pressure comes off.
The discs soak fluid back up and plump out again.
By morning, you're back to full height.
In space, without gravity compressing the spine at all, astronauts can grow up to about three percent taller.
It reverses when they return.
Over decades, discs gradually lose some of their water content, which is one reason people tend to get a little shorter with age.
Your body isn't a statue.
It's a system constantly responding to the forces on it, hour by hour.
Even your height is a daily negotiation with gravity.

Change one word in a question, and you can change what someone remembers seeing.
In 1974, two psychologists proved it with a car crash.
The researchers were Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer.
They showed students short films of traffic accidents, then asked them questions.
The key question was: about how fast were the cars going when they hit each other?
Except for some students, the word hit was swapped.
Smashed.
Collided.
Bumped.
Contacted.
The films were the same.
The answers weren't.
People asked about cars that smashed estimated speeds around forty miles an hour.
People asked about cars that hit gave estimates closer to thirty-four.
Then came the unsettling part.
A week later, the students were asked if they'd seen any broken glass.
There was no broken glass in the film.
But the people who heard the word smashed were more than twice as likely to say yes.
One verb had planted a memory.
Psychologists now think memory works less like a video recording and more like a reconstruction.
Each time you remember something, your brain rebuilds it from pieces, and in that rebuilding, it can be updated, blended or edited.
Researchers call one version of this process reconsolidation.
Even our most vivid memories aren't safe.
After the Challenger space shuttle disaster in 1986, researchers asked students where they were when they heard the news.
Years later they asked again.
Many accounts had changed significantly, yet people felt highly confident in the new version.
Here's the takeaway.
Confidence is a feeling, not proof.
A memory can feel crystal clear and still be wrong.
That's not a flaw in you.
It's how a brain that's built for making sense of the world, rather than archiving it, works.
If your memory edits things on its own, what else is your brain quietly doing behind your back?

The bat costs one pound more than the ball.
How much is the ball?

The ball costs five pence.
If it cost ten, the bat would cost one pound ten, and together they'd be one pound twenty.
The answer that appears instantly feels right, but it isn't.
That puzzle comes from research by the psychologist Shane Frederick, building on the work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky.
Kahneman later popularised a simple way to think about it: two systems of thinking.
System one is fast, automatic and effortless.
It recognises faces, reads emotions and finishes the phrase bread and.
System two is slow, deliberate and lazy.
It does long division and checks your work, but only when it's forced to.
Most of the time, system one is brilliant.
It's why you can drive a familiar route while chatting.
But it runs on shortcuts called heuristics, and shortcuts have blind spots.
In Frederick's studies, around half of students at elite universities like Harvard, MIT and Princeton gave the intuitive wrong answer to the bat and ball question.
Intelligence doesn't switch off the fast system.
One famous shortcut is the availability heuristic.
We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
That's why plane crashes, which are heavily reported, often feel riskier than car journeys, which are statistically far more dangerous per trip for most people.
The goal isn't to stop using your fast brain.
It's to notice when the stakes are high and the answer arrived suspiciously quickly.
That's the moment to make system two do some work.
System one doesn't only shape what you think.
It shapes what you do, every day, on autopilot.
